# Maṇikaṇṭhajātaka (Ja 253)

**ID:** Ja 253
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Maṇikaṇṭhajātaka
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** Jewel-Neck the Dragon King
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ja253
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul2.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Maṇikaṇṭhajātaka* (Ja 253) belongs to the *Yācanavagga* (Chapter on Begging) of the Pali Jātaka collection [Anandajoti 2010]. According to its commentary, the Buddha delivered the story while residing at the Aggāḷava shrine near Āḷavī, occasioned by the training rule on building huts (*Kuṭikārasikkhāpada*) after local monks persistently begged the laity for building supplies until people fled at the sight of them [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1879; Anālayo, Genesis of the bodhisattva ideal]. To teach contentment and the dangers of excessive begging, the Buddha related a tale of the past about the nāga king Maṇikaṇṭha ("Jewel-throat" or "Jewel-neck"), who inhabited the Ganges and could assume human form [Boulton 1982; Bechert et al. 1997]. The nāga formed an intense attachment to an ascetic hermit and embraced him in serpent form; on the advice of his brother (the Bodhisatta), the distressed ascetic repeatedly asked the nāga to give him his wish-granting neck-jewel, prompting the frightened serpent king to depart and never return [Anālayo, Genesis of the bodhisattva ideal; Anandajoti 2010; Gorant, Nāgas in Early Buddhism]. A stone relief on the Bhārhut stupa railing depicting an ascetic conversing with a nāga has been identified with this narrative [Anālayo, Genesis of the bodhisattva ideal; Gorant, Nāgas in Early Buddhism].

Curated parallels and textual analysis link the verses of this Jātaka directly to the Vinaya Piṭaka's *Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga* on *Saṅghādisesa* 6 (Bu-Vb Ss6), which preserves the same verses in a distinct prose context [SuttaCentral; Winternitz 1933; Bechert et al. 1997]. Maurice Winternitz cited this correspondence as critical evidence that the Jātaka verses represent early canonical material, whereas the prose stories are later narrative elaborations [Winternitz 1933]. Related versions of this narrative in connection with the sixth *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rule also appear in non-Theravāda Vinaya traditions, including the Mahāsāṃghika, Mahīśāsaka, and Dharmaguptaka recensions [Bechert et al. 1997]. DharmaNexus matches confirm this internal Pali text reuse, identifying shared segments between Ja 253 (§0.4–2.4) and *Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Saṅghādisesa* 6 (§1.3.34–1.3.42, similarity 0.99), as well as corresponding passages in the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus].

**Parallels and text reuse**

- Passage-level parallels (SuttaCentral): Bu-Vb Ss6 Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Saṅghādisesa 6
- Text reuse within the Pali corpus (DharmaNexus): Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā (Dutiyo bhāgo) (Atk S0513a2) (§0.4–2.4 ↔ §1838_5–1844); Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Saṅghādisesa 6 (Bu-Vb Ss6) (§0.4–2.4 ↔ §1.3.34–1.3.42)

**Sources**

- [SuttaCentral] SuttaCentral record for Ja 253 — Supplied title, English title, blurb, and curated parallel to Bu-Vb Ss6.
- [DharmaNexus] DharmaNexus alignment database — Provided text-reuse data between Ja 253, Bu-Vb Ss6, and the Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā.
- [Anālayo, Genesis of the bodhisattva ideal] Bhikkhu Anālayo, The Genesis of the Bodhisattva Ideal (Abhinav Publications) — Recounted the Vinaya background, the story of the nāga king and the seer's request for the jewel, and noted the Bhārhut railing relief.
- [Anandajoti 2010] Bhikkhu Ānandajoti, Buddhist Wisdom Verses: 551 Verses from the Canon (2010) — Provided chapter placement in Yācanavagga, alternative English title, and narrative summary of the hermit begging for the dragon's jewel.
- [Boulton 1982] Nancy Elizabeth Boulton, Early Chinese Buddhist Travel Records as a Literary Genre (1982) — Noted the nāga king Maṇikaṇṭha's location in the Ganges, his shape-shifting ability, and his magical jewel.
- [Gorant, Nāgas in Early Buddhism] Gorant, Nāgas in Early Buddhism: A Heavenly Abode and an Unfortunate Birth — Discussed the Bhārhut depiction of the conversation between the Bodhisatta's ascetic brother and the nāga king Maṇikaṇṭha.
- [Winternitz 1933] Maurice Winternitz, A History of Indian Literature, Vol. II: Buddhist Literature and Jaina Literature (1933) — Documented that Ja 253 verses appear in the Vinayapiṭaka with different prose, discussing the date and nature of Jātaka prose.

- [Bechert et al. 1997] Heinz Bechert, Sven Bretfeld, and Petra Kieffer-Pülz (eds.), Untersuchungen zur Buddhistischen Literatur (1997) — Surveyed parallel narratives involving the nāgarāja Maṇikaṇṭha in other Vinaya traditions for Saṃghāvaśeṣa 6.
